name: Stephen of Mar Saba
otherNames: Stephen the Sabaite; Stephanus Monachus Sabaita, the Bollandists' Latin heading for him
Stephen the Poet, the title by which the Jerusalem Typikon, the Bollandists report, tells him apart from Stephen the Wonderworker
knownFor: A monk of Mar Saba, near Jerusalem, who saw raiders attack the monastery in the late 700s. At the order of his abbot, Basil, he wrote the account of the twenty monks who died, most of them in a cave filled with smoke.
dates: The raid came in the year of the world 6288, AD 788, in the fifth indiction, by his own account. The Bollandists, the seventeenth-century editors of the Acta Sanctorum, make it 796 in their text. Georg Graf, in 1910, gives March 796 or 797. The Bollandists think Stephen wrote straight after the raiders left, and their margin puts that just after Easter of 797. No source used here gives his birth or death
place: The laura of Saint Sabas, called Mar Saba, near Jerusalem, where he lived and saw the raid. A laura is a monastery of separate cells around a church. No source used here gives his birthplace
role: Monk of Mar Saba; eyewitness and recorder of the raid on the monastery; writer of hymns for its martyrs

keyWorks.title: Passion of the Twenty Martyrs of Mar Saba
keyWorks.about: his eyewitness account, from the civil war among the Arab tribes that laid Palestine waste to the deaths of the twenty and the care of the wounded. The Greek title calls the killers barbarians, that is, Saracens. The Bollandists copied the Greek in 1662 from one manuscript, more than six hundred years old, lent by Pierre Séguier, chancellor of France. They printed it with their own Latin translation. Leaves are missing in places

keyWorks.title: Canon for the twenty martyrs
keyWorks.about: a hymn for the church's office of the twenty, from the Greek Menaia, the monthly service books of the Greek church. The Bollandists give it in Latin and say it is by the same Stephen. Its acrostic, a line spelled by the first letters of its verses, says the writer praises the martyrs in hymns, and carries no name. Stephen himself, at the end of his account, speaks of singing hymns to the martyrs

traces: The Bollandists printed the Greek and their Latin in the Acta Sanctorum for 20 March. They knew no second manuscript to fill the gaps in Séguier's.
The office for 20 March in the printed Menaia is given over wholly to the twenty, the Bollandists say. They credit its canons to Stephen.
remembered: The Life of Stephen the Wonderworker, as the Bollandists report it, calls him the glory and ornament of the whole laura.
The Jerusalem Typikon, the Bollandists say, keeps his feast on 27 October under the title Poet.
Nikodemos the Hagiorite (1748/9 to 1809), in his Greek Synaxaristes, a book of saints' days, tells the twenty fathers' story for 20 March without naming Stephen. He blames Ethiopians called Moors.

uncertain: His name. His account, in Greek and in Latin, never names its author. The name Stephen rests on the Bollandists' heading and commentary, which take it from a Life of Stephen the Wonderworker that is not among the sources used here. Of his own life, only what he says himself is known: he was a monk of Mar Saba, he was there in the raid, he wrote at Abbot Basil's order, and he wrote hymns for the martyrs. He calls himself a sinner and unlearned.

Which Stephen. The Bollandists keep him apart from Stephen the Wonderworker, the nephew of John of Damascus, who they say died before the raid. Their index lists the two as separate men. No source used here makes the writer a relative of John of Damascus.

The year. His account gives the year of the world 6288, AD 788, in the fifth indiction, when Elias was patriarch of Jerusalem and Basil was abbot. The Bollandists, by their own chronology, make it 796 in their text, while their margin has him writing soon after the raid, just after Easter of 797. Their note on the martyr Christopher, a convert from Persia whom Stephen names, puts his death in 789 (the scan reads 189), seven years before the twenty, which also points to 796. Georg Graf, in his 1910 German edition of the Arabic writings of Theodore Abu Qurrah, puts the massacre in March 796 or 797.
The day. The Bollandists place the deaths on 20 March, the Thursday of Holy Week, the day the feast is kept.
When he wrote. The Bollandists think he wrote straight after the raiders left, when Abbot Basil, who had been away, came back. Their margin puts it after Easter of 797.

Who the raiders were. Stephen sets the raid in a civil war among the Arab tribes of Palestine. The Menologion printed by Canisius and the Typikon, the Bollandists report, blame Ethiopians or Moors. The Bollandists answer that these were only some of the killers, acting under Arab masters. Nikodemos the Hagiorite names Ethiopians called Moors. Georg Graf calls them Bedouin.
What he did not see. Stephen marks his hearsay. Sergius of Damascus's last words came from a brother caught with him, and one miracle from a priest he calls most worthy of trust.
